sentences.text: The holotype specimen — the specific fossil the species is based on — represents a small animal less than one meter long, though researchers estimate the adult reached about 2 meters and weighed 20 kilograms.
Its foot structure followed a toe formula of 2-3-4-5-0, indicating a specific arrangement of digits on each limb.
Anatomical analysis shows that the perone bone does not touch the calcaneus at the bottom of the leg.
The animal possessed a unique prepubic process shaped like a rod with a widened and rotated front end.
The first chevron of its tail forms a distinct right angle between its top and bottom parts, unlike the gradual curve seen in other ornithopods.
A short ascending process on its jumping leg extended past the front of the tibia.
Amateur paleontologist José María Herrero Marzo and his son discovered the remains near Galve, Spain, in 1982.
The genus Gideonmantellia and the species Gideonmantellia amosanjuanae were validly named in 2012 by a team led by Ruiz-Omeñaca.
The genus name honors Gideon Mantell, the first describer of Hypsilophodon, while the species name honors the paleontologist Olga María Amo Sanjuán.
To date, only one fossil occurrence of this dinosaur has been recorded.
In this animal, the sacral vertebrae were not yet fused into a sacrum.
The prepubic process rotates strongly around its longitudinal axis, with the side turned 52 degrees upward.
Gideonmantellia is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
It is classified as a basal member of the group Ornithopoda, and a 2017 study by Madzia et al. identified it as the most basal ornithopod.
The species belongs to the family Hypsilophodontidae.
This creature lived during the Early Cretaceous Barremian stage in what is now Spain.
The Barremian stage occurred between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago.
Between 1995 and 2001, Gideonmantellia was assigned to the family Hypsilophodontidae before its current classification was established.
